title: Literature May Help People Be More Forgiving — Study
paragraphs: Forgiving someone who has hurt us can be very difficult. But according to a new study, reading stories may help people become more forgiving in real life, as long as the stories are written in a particular way.

The study was carried out by researchers at Ohio State University in the US, including Angus Fletcher, a professor of English, and Mark Matthews, who recently earned a PhD in social psychology. It was published in October 2026 in the journal Frontiers in Psychology.

The researchers carried out three studies with a total of 1,563 participants. The participants read a short story about an elderly woman named Mary, who adopts a puppy at the age of 85. Mary hires a repairman and asks him to keep the door closed. However, he leaves the door open, and the puppy escapes.

The researchers then tested a writing technique called "internal focalization." This means that the reader can see what a character is thinking. In one version of the story, readers could see the repairman's private thoughts of regret. In another version, he said the same words of regret out loud to another character.

The results showed that when readers could see the repairman's private regret, they were more likely to forgive him. More surprisingly, people who forgave the character in the story were also more likely to forgive people who had hurt them in real life.

Fletcher explained that if people just read a story without this technique, they are not likely to forgive a character. Matthews said that readers can feel that the character's regret is sincere. Fletcher also pointed out that one great thing about literature is that people do not need to be in a crisis to benefit from it.
However, the study has some limits. The researchers only measured forgiveness right after people read the story, so it is not clear if the effect lasts.
